Pontiff
pŏn´tĭf
n. (a high priest; in Roman usage, the pope, styled pontifex maximus)
Latin pontifex, literally bridge-builder, the title of the chief priest of pagan Rome; taken over by the bishops of Rome after the empire became Christian.

Biblical Definition

A pontiff is a high priest, and the word carries its own argument: the title pontifex maximus belonged to the chief priest of the Roman state religion before it was assumed by the bishop of Rome. Scripture knows one High Priest under the new covenant — “we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God” (Heb 4:14) — whose priesthood is unchangeable “because he continueth ever” (Heb 7:24), and one bridge between God and men, “the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5). Every believer is a priest in Him: “ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood” (1Pe 2:5).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines pontiff as a high priest; and applies the term particularly to the pope, the sovereign pontiff.

expand to see more

PONTIFF, n. A high priest. The Jews had one high priest, who officiated in the temple.

2. The pope, so called from his being the chief priest of the Romish church.

Key Scripture

Heb 4:14 — "Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession."

Heb 7:24 — "But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood."

1Ti 2:5 — "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;"

1Pe 2:5 — "Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ."

Heb 7:27 — "Who needeth not daily, as those high priests, to offer up sacrifice, first for his own sins, and then for the people's: for this he did once, when he offered up himself."

Modern Corruption

A standing human priesthood is maintained under the new covenant, and Hebrews argues that the priesthood which continueth ever admits no successor.

expand to see more

The letter to the Hebrews spends four chapters on a single point: the old priests were many, “because they were not suffered to continue by reason of death” (Heb 7:23), and Christ has an unchangeable priesthood because He continueth ever. A succession is what mortality requires; the whole force of the argument is that His does not require one. To install a standing human pontiff under the new covenant is not to supplement that priesthood but to contradict the reason Hebrews gives for its finality.

The word's history is its own commentary. Pontifex maximus was the office of the emperor as head of Rome's state religion, and the church that took the title also took a good deal of the apparatus — the vestments, the calendar, the altars, the mediating caste. The Reformers' complaint was not aesthetic. A priest is a man who stands between, and where a priest stands between, the veil that was rent from the top to the bottom (Mat 27:51) has been quietly sewn up again. First Peter 2:5 gives the only priesthood the new covenant knows besides Christ's, and it is the whole congregation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek archiereus (G749), high priest; hiereus (G2409), priest; mesites (G3316), mediator; Latin pontifex, bridge-builder, chief priest.

expand to see more

Greek archiereus (G749) — high priest; Hebrews 2:17, 4:14–15, 7:26, 9:11.

Greek hierateuma (G2406) — a priesthood; 1 Peter 2:5, 2:9, of the whole church.

Greek mesites (G3316) — mediator; 1 Timothy 2:5, Hebrews 8:6, 9:15, 12:24.

Usage

"“He continueth ever” — the reason His priesthood admits no successor."

"“One mediator between God and men” — the only bridge the word claims to name."

"“An holy priesthood” — said of the congregation, not a caste."
